texts.0: On a cold February morning in 1912, a six-year-old boy sat on the Dragon Throne for the last time while adults around him signed away three centuries of imperial rule. The story of how that moment arrived — and what came after — is the story of the Qing dynasty: the last imperial dynasty of China, the longest-lived in the modern era, and one of the most dramatic arcs in all of human history.
texts.1:
## Origins in Manchuria: Nurhaci Unifies the Jurchen Clans (1616)
Origins in Manchuria: Nurhaci Unifies the Jurchen Clans (1616) (Powered by AI)
Deep in the forests of Manchuria, far from the silks and bureaucrats of Beijing, a Jurchen tribal leader named Nurhaci did something audacious: he unified the rival clans of his people, declared a new dynasty he called the Later Jin, and began building the military and administrative machine that would eventually swallow China whole. His people — soon to rename themselves Manchus — were horsemen, hunters, and warriors who had spent generations living at the cold edge of the Ming Empire’s northern frontier, dismissed as peripheral by the sophisticated court culture to their south.
To bind his forces together, Nurhaci organised them into the Eight Banners, a system that was equal parts army, census, and identity document. Every Manchu man, woman, and child was enrolled in a Banner; it determined where they fought, where they lived, and who they were. That structure would remain the skeleton of Qing power for nearly three hundred years — a remarkable feat of institutional endurance that originated in a northeast forest long before anyone imagined Manchus sitting on the Dragon Throne in Beijing.

## The Dragon Throne Changes Hands in a Season of Chaos (1644)
Rebel forces entering Beijing in 1644, of the kind that toppled the Ming dynasty and opened the door to 300 years of Qing rule. (Powered by AI)
The Ming dynasty did not fall to the Manchus — not exactly. It fell first to itself. A peasant rebel army under Li Zicheng stormed Beijing in the spring of 1644, and the last Ming emperor, rather than surrender, hanged himself from a tree on Coal Hill overlooking the Forbidden City. Into that power vacuum, Manchu forces poured through the Great Wall and seized the capital within weeks, presenting their conquest not as an invasion but as the restoration of order that the Ming had catastrophically failed to maintain.
The Qing dynasty officially began its rule over China proper in 1644, inaugurating what would become the country’s final imperial dynasty. The new rulers were keenly aware of their outsider status, and they enforced cultural submission with brutal directness: Han Chinese men were ordered to shave their foreheads and adopt the Manchu queue hairstyle or face execution. A braid, in other words, became a loyalty oath worn on the body — a visible, daily declaration of submission to the new order.

texts.3:
## The Kangxi Emperor Builds an Empire (1661-1722)
The Kangxi Emperor seated on his throne in full imperial court dress, Qing dynasty. — AnonymousUnknown author Qing Dynasty Court Painter · Public domain
He took the throne at age seven — a child emperor in a dynasty that had a recurring and consequential habit of placing boys in impossible seats of power — but Kangxi grew into one of the most formidable rulers of his era. Over sixty-one years on the throne, the longest reign in Chinese imperial history, he brought Taiwan, Mongolia, Tibet, and vast territories in Central Asia into the Qing Empire, forging borders that roughly correspond to the footprint of modern China today.
His court was not merely a military enterprise. Kangxi welcomed Jesuit astronomers, commissioned monumental encyclopaedias, and engaged in scientific correspondence with Enlightenment Europe, cultivating the image of a cosmopolitan empire at the height of its self-confidence. By the mid-eighteenth century, under his grandson the Qianlong Emperor, the Great Qing was among the wealthiest and most populous states on earth, accounting for roughly a third of global economic output. The distance between that peak and what came next makes the dynasty’s eventual collapse all the more vertiginous.

texts.4:
## Opium, Gunboats, and the First Crack in the Wall (1839-1842)
A scene from the 1839 Opium War crisis, as confiscated British opium burns at Guangzhou while warships gather offshore (Powered by AI)
When a Qing official ordered the destruction of more than twenty thousand chests of British opium at Guangzhou in 1839, the act seemed like one of sovereign confidence. Britain’s response — naval bombardment, amphibious landings, and the systematic dismantling of Qing coastal defences — revealed something far more alarming. China’s military, formidable against steppe opponents, had no answer for iron steamships and modern artillery. The defeat was swift, decisive, and deeply unsettling to those paying attention inside the empire.
The Treaty of Nanking that ended the First Opium War forced China to cede Hong Kong Island to Britain, open five treaty ports to foreign commerce, and pay a substantial indemnity. It was the opening blow in what Chinese historians would later call the “century of national humiliation,” and it exposed a technological and organisational gap between Qing forces and industrialising Western powers that reformers would spend the next seventy years frantically, and ultimately unsuccessfully, trying to close.

texts.5:
## The Taiping Rebellion Nearly Tears the Dynasty Apart (1850-1864)
Chinese ink illustration showing imperial troops advancing through mountainous terrain during a military campaign. — Library of Congress
The most devastating civil war in recorded history began with a man who believed he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ. Hong Xiuquan, a Hakka schoolteacher who had repeatedly failed the imperial civil service examinations, raised a millenarian army that captured Nanjing in 1853 and held it for eleven years. Estimates of the Taiping Rebellion’s death toll range from twenty to thirty million people — exceeding the total fatalities of the First World War — and the conflict left swaths of southern China in physical and economic ruin.
What made the uprising existentially dangerous for the Qing was not only the bloodshed but the political concession required to suppress it. The dynasty’s own Banner armies proved incapable of crushing the rebellion, forcing Beijing to empower regional Han Chinese militias commanded by local strongmen such as Zeng Guofan. Real military authority, for the first time in the dynasty’s history, was migrating away from the Manchu imperial centre toward the provinces. The Qing survived, but it survived hollowed out — its treasury depleted, its armies discredited, and its structural authority quietly fractured in ways that would prove fatal in the decades ahead.

## One Hundred Days of Reform, Then a Coup (1898)
One Hundred Days of Reform, Then a Coup (1898) (Powered by AI)
In the summer of 1898, the young Guangxu Emperor looked at what Meiji Japan had accomplished through rapid, top-down modernisation and determined that China would follow the same path. Over a frantic hundred and three days he issued a cascade of edicts remaking the civil service examination system, the military, and the structure of education — reform at a pace that alarmed virtually every established interest in the empire. The figure with the power to stop him was not a general or a rival minister. It was his aunt.
The Empress Dowager Cixi staged a palace coup, placed Guangxu under house arrest on an island within the Forbidden City’s lake, and methodically reversed his reforms. He would remain her prisoner for a decade, dying on November 14, 1908 — one day before Cixi herself, in circumstances historians continue to debate; a 2008 forensic study found elevated arsenic levels in Guangxu’s remains, suggesting poisoning. The episode delivered an unambiguous message to a generation of Chinese reformers: the dynasty could not save itself from within. Those who absorbed that lesson most thoroughly would spend the next thirteen years building a revolution.

texts.7:
## A Mutiny in Wuhan Topples an Empire in Weeks (October 1911)
The end began not with a grand revolutionary army marching on Beijing but with an accidental explosion in a Wuhan safe house that forced a group of conspirators to launch their uprising before their preparations were complete. On October 10, 1911 — now commemorated in Taiwan as Double Ten Day — a garrison mutiny in Wuchang set off a chain reaction the Qing dynasty had no capacity to contain. Within six weeks, fifteen of China’s twenty-four provinces had declared independence from imperial rule.
The fall of the Qing dynasty was not decided by a siege or a climactic battle — it was a haemorrhage of loyalty. Provincial elites, military commanders, and career officials who had spent their working lives in the dynasty’s service simply stopped defending the centre, calculating that the dynasty was finished and that their futures lay elsewhere. Sun Yat-sen, the revolution’s most prominent figurehead, was in the United States when he learned that his movement had succeeded. The empire of nearly three centuries dissolved, in the end, less like a fortress stormed than like ice quietly melting in a warming room.

Title: A Six-Year-Old Lost the Dragon Throne and Ended 300 Years of Qing Rule

On a cold February morning in 1912, a six-year-old boy sat on the Dragon Throne for the last time while adults around him signed away three centuries of imperial rule. The story of how that moment arrived — and what came after — is the story of the Qing dynasty: the last imperial dynasty of China, the longest-lived in the modern era, and one of the most dramatic arcs in all of human history.

## Origins in Manchuria: Nurhaci Unifies the Jurchen Clans (1616)
Origins in Manchuria: Nurhaci Unifies the Jurchen Clans (1616) (Powered by AI)
Deep in the forests of Manchuria, far from the silks and bureaucrats of Beijing, a Jurchen tribal leader named Nurhaci did something audacious: he unified the rival clans of his people, declared a new dynasty he called the Later Jin, and began building the military and administrative machine that would eventually swallow China whole. His people — soon to rename themselves Manchus — were horsemen, hunters, and warriors who had spent generations living at the cold edge of the Ming Empire’s northern frontier, dismissed as peripheral by the sophisticated court culture to their south.
To bind his forces together, Nurhaci organised them into the Eight Banners, a system that was equal parts army, census, and identity document. Every Manchu man, woman, and child was enrolled in a Banner; it determined where they fought, where they lived, and who they were. That structure would remain the skeleton of Qing power for nearly three hundred years — a remarkable feat of institutional endurance that originated in a northeast forest long before anyone imagined Manchus sitting on the Dragon Throne in Beijing.

## The Dragon Throne Changes Hands in a Season of Chaos (1644)
Rebel forces entering Beijing in 1644, of the kind that toppled the Ming dynasty and opened the door to 300 years of Qing rule. (Powered by AI)
The Ming dynasty did not fall to the Manchus — not exactly. It fell first to itself. A peasant rebel army under Li Zicheng stormed Beijing in the spring of 1644, and the last Ming emperor, rather than surrender, hanged himself from a tree on Coal Hill overlooking the Forbidden City. Into that power vacuum, Manchu forces poured through the Great Wall and seized the capital within weeks, presenting their conquest not as an invasion but as the restoration of order that the Ming had catastrophically failed to maintain.
The Qing dynasty officially began its rule over China proper in 1644, inaugurating what would become the country’s final imperial dynasty. The new rulers were keenly aware of their outsider status, and they enforced cultural submission with brutal directness: Han Chinese men were ordered to shave their foreheads and adopt the Manchu queue hairstyle or face execution. A braid, in other words, became a loyalty oath worn on the body — a visible, daily declaration of submission to the new order.

## The Kangxi Emperor Builds an Empire (1661-1722)
The Kangxi Emperor seated on his throne in full imperial court dress, Qing dynasty. — AnonymousUnknown author Qing Dynasty Court Painter · Public domain
He took the throne at age seven — a child emperor in a dynasty that had a recurring and consequential habit of placing boys in impossible seats of power — but Kangxi grew into one of the most formidable rulers of his era. Over sixty-one years on the throne, the longest reign in Chinese imperial history, he brought Taiwan, Mongolia, Tibet, and vast territories in Central Asia into the Qing Empire, forging borders that roughly correspond to the footprint of modern China today.
His court was not merely a military enterprise. Kangxi welcomed Jesuit astronomers, commissioned monumental encyclopaedias, and engaged in scientific correspondence with Enlightenment Europe, cultivating the image of a cosmopolitan empire at the height of its self-confidence. By the mid-eighteenth century, under his grandson the Qianlong Emperor, the Great Qing was among the wealthiest and most populous states on earth, accounting for roughly a third of global economic output. The distance between that peak and what came next makes the dynasty’s eventual collapse all the more vertiginous.

## Opium, Gunboats, and the First Crack in the Wall (1839-1842)
A scene from the 1839 Opium War crisis, as confiscated British opium burns at Guangzhou while warships gather offshore (Powered by AI)
When a Qing official ordered the destruction of more than twenty thousand chests of British opium at Guangzhou in 1839, the act seemed like one of sovereign confidence. Britain’s response — naval bombardment, amphibious landings, and the systematic dismantling of Qing coastal defences — revealed something far more alarming. China’s military, formidable against steppe opponents, had no answer for iron steamships and modern artillery. The defeat was swift, decisive, and deeply unsettling to those paying attention inside the empire.
The Treaty of Nanking that ended the First Opium War forced China to cede Hong Kong Island to Britain, open five treaty ports to foreign commerce, and pay a substantial indemnity. It was the opening blow in what Chinese historians would later call the “century of national humiliation,” and it exposed a technological and organisational gap between Qing forces and industrialising Western powers that reformers would spend the next seventy years frantically, and ultimately unsuccessfully, trying to close.

## The Taiping Rebellion Nearly Tears the Dynasty Apart (1850-1864)
Chinese ink illustration showing imperial troops advancing through mountainous terrain during a military campaign. — Library of Congress
The most devastating civil war in recorded history began with a man who believed he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ. Hong Xiuquan, a Hakka schoolteacher who had repeatedly failed the imperial civil service examinations, raised a millenarian army that captured Nanjing in 1853 and held it for eleven years. Estimates of the Taiping Rebellion’s death toll range from twenty to thirty million people — exceeding the total fatalities of the First World War — and the conflict left swaths of southern China in physical and economic ruin.
What made the uprising existentially dangerous for the Qing was not only the bloodshed but the political concession required to suppress it. The dynasty’s own Banner armies proved incapable of crushing the rebellion, forcing Beijing to empower regional Han Chinese militias commanded by local strongmen such as Zeng Guofan. Real military authority, for the first time in the dynasty’s history, was migrating away from the Manchu imperial centre toward the provinces. The Qing survived, but it survived hollowed out — its treasury depleted, its armies discredited, and its structural authority quietly fractured in ways that would prove fatal in the decades ahead.

## One Hundred Days of Reform, Then a Coup (1898)
One Hundred Days of Reform, Then a Coup (1898) (Powered by AI)
In the summer of 1898, the young Guangxu Emperor looked at what Meiji Japan had accomplished through rapid, top-down modernisation and determined that China would follow the same path. Over a frantic hundred and three days he issued a cascade of edicts remaking the civil service examination system, the military, and the structure of education — reform at a pace that alarmed virtually every established interest in the empire. The figure with the power to stop him was not a general or a rival minister. It was his aunt.
The Empress Dowager Cixi staged a palace coup, placed Guangxu under house arrest on an island within the Forbidden City’s lake, and methodically reversed his reforms. He would remain her prisoner for a decade, dying on November 14, 1908 — one day before Cixi herself, in circumstances historians continue to debate; a 2008 forensic study found elevated arsenic levels in Guangxu’s remains, suggesting poisoning. The episode delivered an unambiguous message to a generation of Chinese reformers: the dynasty could not save itself from within. Those who absorbed that lesson most thoroughly would spend the next thirteen years building a revolution.

## A Mutiny in Wuhan Topples an Empire in Weeks (October 1911)
The end began not with a grand revolutionary army marching on Beijing but with an accidental explosion in a Wuhan safe house that forced a group of conspirators to launch their uprising before their preparations were complete. On October 10, 1911 — now commemorated in Taiwan as Double Ten Day — a garrison mutiny in Wuchang set off a chain reaction the Qing dynasty had no capacity to contain. Within six weeks, fifteen of China’s twenty-four provinces had declared independence from imperial rule.
The fall of the Qing dynasty was not decided by a siege or a climactic battle — it was a haemorrhage of loyalty. Provincial elites, military commanders, and career officials who had spent their working lives in the dynasty’s service simply stopped defending the centre, calculating that the dynasty was finished and that their futures lay elsewhere. Sun Yat-sen, the revolution’s most prominent figurehead, was in the United States when he learned that his movement had succeeded. The empire of nearly three centuries dissolved, in the end, less like a fortress stormed than like ice quietly melting in a warming room.

During the Western Han Dynasty, a Guangling County was established in the area that is now Huaian. During the Three Kingdoms period (in the state of Wu), Guangling County was placed in the area that is now Yangzhou, which is how the modern Guangling name came to be.

Title: Experiencing new charm of ancient city
Chunks: 0,1,2
[Photo provided to Women of China]
Yangzhou is located in the central region of East China's Jiangsu province, where the Yangtze River meets the Grand Canal. It is known as "the first canal city in China." Yangzhou, with a history of more than 2,500 years, was one of the first cities to be designated a national historical and cultural city by the State Council.
**Built by water**
Yangzhou's development has remained inextricably intertwined with the Grand Canal since the canal was built more than 2,500 years ago. Yangzhou has shared provenance with the canal, which stretches from Beijing to Hangzhou, capital of East China's Zhejiang province.
The Grand Canal was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2014. The office for the canal's World Heritage site application was established in Yangzhou in 2006. Gu Feng, then-head of Yangzhou's cultural heritage bureau, and the office's director, says one of the greatest values of Yangzhou's section of the canal is that it has an accurate historical record.
According to China's first detailed historical compendium, Zuo Zhuan, King Fuchai of the Wu Kingdom constructed a city, known as Hancheng, and a canal, called Han Gou, which connected the Yangtze and Huaihe rivers in 486 BC. Hancheng eventually became Yangzhou, and the construction of canals in other eras, including the Sui (581-618) and Yuan (1206-1368) dynasties, eventually completed the Grand Canal.
[Photo provided to Women of China]
The Yangzhou section of the Grand Canal hosts rich cultural heritage. Since the Grand Canal was added to UNESCO's World Heritage list in 2014, six channels and 10 heritage sites from Yangzhou have received UNESCO world-heritage status.
Slender West Lake, one of Yangzhou's most-renowned scenic spots, is linked with the Grand Canal, and the lake is one of UNESCO's World Heritage sites along the canal.
The canal brought economic prosperity and cultural progress to Yangzhou. Historical records from the Tang (618-907) and Song (960-1279) dynasties describe Yangzhou as one of the country's most affluent cities.

Although the canal was constructed for military purposes, it later facilitated the national food supply, including grain and salt. Yangzhou was, therefore, home to many salt merchants, who built elaborate Chinese gardens, which remain to this day.
Yangzhou China Grand Canal Museum, which opened in 2021, is designed to be an "encyclopedia" of the canal, showcasing relevant culture, economics and ecology by using immersive technology and an interactive design.
Yangzhou has hosted various canal-related events, including the World Canal Cities Forum and the World Canals Conference, both of which focus on international exchanges related to the preservation of canals, and the Grand Canal Culture and Tourism Expo, which features parades on the waterway.
**Historical, cultural blocks**
Yangzhou was called Guangling during ancient times. Guangling district, in the central area of Yangzhou, is known for ancient blocks built during the Ming (1368-1644) and Qing (1616-1911) dynasties.
There are four well-preserved historical and cultural blocks — Dongguan Street, Renfengli, Wanzi Street and Nanhexia — in Guangling, and combined they are home to more than 500 historical buildings, and 148 cultural-relic-protection units.
Dongguan street, which is 1,122 meters long, has been a historical witness to the development and evolution of Yangzhou, and it has been a window that has displayed the city's canal and salt-merchant cultures. It used to be a gateway of water transportation, and a center of business, religion and culture. It boasted a bustling market and various stores.
Dongguan street has a fish-bone-styled street layout, which maintains the traditional style and features of the Ming and Qing dynasties. Scattered throughout the block are former residences of historic figures, mansions of former salt merchants, and temples and gardens. With rich historical relics and cultural remains, Dongguan street is among the best-preserved ancient commercial streets of the cities along the Grand Canal.
Dongguan street, home to catering and entertainment venues, gardens, museums, time-honored stores, and ancient residential buildings, is one of the best places for Chinese and foreigners to appreciate the history, culture and lifestyle of Yangzhou.

The Ministry of Culture and Tourism of China on March 1 issued an announcement that Dongguan Street was officially approved as one of the second group of national tourism and leisure blocks.
[Photo provided to Women of China]
**New vitality**
The authorities in Yangzhou have renovated historical and cultural communities while at the same time they have maintained traditions and the city's cultural charm. Nowadays, the ancient streets and alleys glow with new vitality, as they have become great options for locals and tourists alike to enjoy their leisure time.
Many domestic and international brands have established their first stores or flagship stores in Yangzhou's historic and cultural communities, and those businesses have injected new impetus into retail sales within the city. The thriving, first-store economy and nighttime economy have become new drivers of local consumption and cultural-tourism development.
Various cultural and tourism festivals have been held, and such events have enriched people's experiences on the city's ancient streets. Such events have included the coffee culture festival, on Pishi Street, and the folk culture festival, in Renfengli community (to mark Dragon Boat Festival).
[Photo provided to Women of China]
Renfengli is the only well-preserved ancient community in Yangzhou that retains the pattern of streets and alleys of the Tang Dynasty. While wandering in Renfengli, tourists will experience the charm of Yangzhou's rich intangible cultural heritage, including Yangzhou paper-cuts, woodblock printing, Yangzhou pinghua (a kind of storytelling in the Yangzhou dialect), and Yangzhou puppet show.
Joseph Simlinck, a Brazilian in his 60s, has a passion for the ancient city of Yangzhou. He and one of his Chinese friends, Gao Hailin, run a Western-style restaurant in Renfengli. Yuan Li, a neighbor of Simlinck, shares that passion for Renfengli. "I am a native of Yangzhou, and I used to work in Shanghai. I moved back to the alley, where I used to live, after I retired. I am impressed by the new look of Renfengli, with both cultural heritage and modern vitality," Yuan says.
_Photos by Yuan Yuhua_
(Source: Women of China English Monthly April 2023 issue)

Yangzhou is located in the central region of East China's Jiangsu province, where the Yangtze River meets the Grand Canal. It is known as "the first canal city in China." Yangzhou, with a history of more than 2,500 years, was one of the first cities to be designated a national historical and cultural city by the State Council.
**Built by water**
Yangzhou's development has remained inextricably intertwined with the Grand Canal since the canal was built more than 2,500 years ago. Yangzhou has shared provenance with the canal, which stretches from Beijing to Hangzhou, capital of East China's Zhejiang province.
The Grand Canal was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2014. The office for the canal's World Heritage site application was established in Yangzhou in 2006. Gu Feng, then-head of Yangzhou's cultural heritage bureau, and the office's director, says one of the greatest values of Yangzhou's section of the canal is that it has an accurate historical record.
According to China's first detailed historical compendium, Zuo Zhuan, King Fuchai of the Wu Kingdom constructed a city, known as Hancheng, and a canal, called Han Gou, which connected the Yangtze and Huaihe rivers in 486 BC. Hancheng eventually became Yangzhou, and the construction of canals in other eras, including the Sui (581-618) and Yuan (1206-1368) dynasties, eventually completed the Grand Canal.
[Photo provided to Women of China]
The Yangzhou section of the Grand Canal hosts rich cultural heritage. Since the Grand Canal was added to UNESCO's World Heritage list in 2014, six channels and 10 heritage sites from Yangzhou have received UNESCO world-heritage status.
Slender West Lake, one of Yangzhou's most-renowned scenic spots, is linked with the Grand Canal, and the lake is one of UNESCO's World Heritage sites along the canal.
The canal brought economic prosperity and cultural progress to Yangzhou. Historical records from the Tang (618-907) and Song (960-1279) dynasties describe Yangzhou as one of the country's most affluent cities.
texts.1:
Although the canal was constructed for military purposes, it later facilitated the national food supply, including grain and salt. Yangzhou was, therefore, home to many salt merchants, who built elaborate Chinese gardens, which remain to this day.
Yangzhou China Grand Canal Museum, which opened in 2021, is designed to be an "encyclopedia" of the canal, showcasing relevant culture, economics and ecology by using immersive technology and an interactive design.
Yangzhou has hosted various canal-related events, including the World Canal Cities Forum and the World Canals Conference, both of which focus on international exchanges related to the preservation of canals, and the Grand Canal Culture and Tourism Expo, which features parades on the waterway.
**Historical, cultural blocks**
Yangzhou was called Guangling during ancient times. Guangling district, in the central area of Yangzhou, is known for ancient blocks built during the Ming (1368-1644) and Qing (1616-1911) dynasties.
There are four well-preserved historical and cultural blocks — Dongguan Street, Renfengli, Wanzi Street and Nanhexia — in Guangling, and combined they are home to more than 500 historical buildings, and 148 cultural-relic-protection units.
Dongguan street, which is 1,122 meters long, has been a historical witness to the development and evolution of Yangzhou, and it has been a window that has displayed the city's canal and salt-merchant cultures. It used to be a gateway of water transportation, and a center of business, religion and culture. It boasted a bustling market and various stores.
Dongguan street has a fish-bone-styled street layout, which maintains the traditional style and features of the Ming and Qing dynasties. Scattered throughout the block are former residences of historic figures, mansions of former salt merchants, and temples and gardens. With rich historical relics and cultural remains, Dongguan street is among the best-preserved ancient commercial streets of the cities along the Grand Canal.
Dongguan street, home to catering and entertainment venues, gardens, museums, time-honored stores, and ancient residential buildings, is one of the best places for Chinese and foreigners to appreciate the history, culture and lifestyle of Yangzhou.
texts.2:
The Ministry of Culture and Tourism of China on March 1 issued an announcement that Dongguan Street was officially approved as one of the second group of national tourism and leisure blocks.
[Photo provided to Women of China]
**New vitality**
The authorities in Yangzhou have renovated historical and cultural communities while at the same time they have maintained traditions and the city's cultural charm. Nowadays, the ancient streets and alleys glow with new vitality, as they have become great options for locals and tourists alike to enjoy their leisure time.
Many domestic and international brands have established their first stores or flagship stores in Yangzhou's historic and cultural communities, and those businesses have injected new impetus into retail sales within the city. The thriving, first-store economy and nighttime economy have become new drivers of local consumption and cultural-tourism development.
Various cultural and tourism festivals have been held, and such events have enriched people's experiences on the city's ancient streets. Such events have included the coffee culture festival, on Pishi Street, and the folk culture festival, in Renfengli community (to mark Dragon Boat Festival).
[Photo provided to Women of China]
Renfengli is the only well-preserved ancient community in Yangzhou that retains the pattern of streets and alleys of the Tang Dynasty. While wandering in Renfengli, tourists will experience the charm of Yangzhou's rich intangible cultural heritage, including Yangzhou paper-cuts, woodblock printing, Yangzhou pinghua (a kind of storytelling in the Yangzhou dialect), and Yangzhou puppet show.
Joseph Simlinck, a Brazilian in his 60s, has a passion for the ancient city of Yangzhou. He and one of his Chinese friends, Gao Hailin, run a Western-style restaurant in Renfengli. Yuan Li, a neighbor of Simlinck, shares that passion for Renfengli. "I am a native of Yangzhou, and I used to work in Shanghai. I moved back to the alley, where I used to live, after I retired. I am impressed by the new look of Renfengli, with both cultural heritage and modern vitality," Yuan says.

Yangzhou was called Guangling during ancient times. Guangling district, in the central area of Yangzhou, is known for ancient blocks built during the Ming (1368-1644) and Qing (1616-1911) dynasties.

It used to be a gateway of water transportation, and a center of business, religion and culture. It boasted a bustling market and various stores.
Dongguan street has a fish-bone-styled street layout, which maintains the traditional style and features of the Ming and Qing dynasties. Scattered throughout the block are former residences of historic figures, mansions of former salt merchants, and temples and gardens. With rich historical relics and cultural remains, Dongguan street is among the best-preserved ancient commercial streets of the cities along the Grand Canal.
Dongguan street, home to catering and entertainment venues, gardens, museums, time-honored stores, and ancient residential buildings, is one of the best places for Chinese and foreigners to appreciate the history, culture and lifestyle of Yangzhou.

The Ministry of Culture and Tourism of China on March 1 issued an announcement that Dongguan Street was officially approved as one of the second group of national tourism and leisure blocks.

The authorities in Yangzhou have renovated historical and cultural communities while at the same time they have maintained traditions and the city's cultural charm. Nowadays, the ancient streets and alleys glow with new vitality, as they have become great options for locals and tourists alike to enjoy their leisure time.

The thriving, first-store economy and nighttime economy have become new drivers of local consumption and cultural-tourism development.
Various cultural and tourism festivals have been held, and such events have enriched people's experiences on the city's ancient streets. Such events have included the coffee culture festival, on Pishi Street, and the folk culture festival, in Renfengli community (to mark Dragon Boat Festival).
[Photo provided to Women of China]
Renfengli is the only well-preserved ancient community in Yangzhou that retains the pattern of streets and alleys of the Tang Dynasty. While wandering in Renfengli, tourists will experience the charm of Yangzhou's rich intangible cultural heritage, including Yangzhou paper-cuts, woodblock printing, Yangzhou pinghua (a kind of storytelling in the Yangzhou dialect), and Yangzhou puppet show.
Joseph Simlinck, a Brazilian in his 60s, has a passion for the ancient city of Yangzhou. He and one of his Chinese friends, Gao Hailin, run a Western-style restaurant in Renfengli. Yuan Li, a neighbor of Simlinck, shares that passion for Renfengli. "I am a native of Yangzhou, and I used to work in Shanghai. I moved back to the alley, where I used to live, after I retired. I am impressed by the new look of Renfengli, with both cultural heritage and modern vitality," Yuan says.
